title: Week 115 · Lesson 139: Adolescent Health, Confidentiality & Risk Assessment — FNP-Level Preventive and Safety Care
html:
PHASE 5 · FAMILY & LIFESPAN PRIMARY CARE

Week 115 — Lesson 139: Adolescent Health, Confidentiality & Risk Assessment

FNP-level goal: Build a confidential, developmentally appropriate adolescent encounter; integrate preventive care with mental health, substance use, sexual health, eating and body concerns, safety, chronic-disease transition, and family strengths; understand legal limits; and respond immediately to suicide, abuse, trafficking, violence, pregnancy emergency, or medical instability.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain confidentiality and its limits clearly to adolescents and caregivers and provide routine private time.
  • Conduct a strength-based psychosocial assessment without making identity or behavior assumptions.
  • Apply current preventive, immunization, depression, suicide, substance-use, and STI screening guidance.
  • Recognize eating-disorder instability, exploitation, abuse, reproductive emergency, and acute psychiatric danger.
  • Create a closed-loop plan that protects privacy across portals, billing, laboratories, pharmacy, and referrals.

Part 1 — Adolescence Is a Clinical Transition

Adolescence includes rapid biologic, cognitive, emotional, social, and identity development. The FNP supports growing autonomy while maintaining family partnership and safety. Begin with strengths: what is going well, who supports the young person, what goals matter, and where they feel safe.

A respectful encounter improves disclosure and future care. Avoid assumptions about sexual orientation, gender identity, sexual activity, substance use, family structure, or ability based on appearance.

Part 2 — Explain Confidentiality Before Sensitive Questions

Tell both caregiver and adolescent that private time is a routine part of adolescent care. Explain what will remain private and the limits: imminent danger, suspected abuse or neglect, certain reportable infections, and other jurisdiction-specific duties. Encourage supportive family communication when safe without making privacy conditional on disclosure.

Consent and confidentiality laws vary by state and service, including reproductive, STI, mental-health, and substance-use care. Know the rules where you practice. Never promise absolute secrecy.

Part 3 — Privacy Is More Than Closing the Door

Portal proxy access, after-visit summaries, automated messages, pharmacy notices, lab labels, scheduling, and insurance explanations of benefits can reveal sensitive care. Ask what phone, email, and portal are safe. Segment records and suppress disclosure only as law and system policy allow.

AAP policy emphasizes that confidentiality is essential to high-quality adolescent care and recommends consistent private time plus systems that protect sensitive information. Document confidentiality discussions without exposing unnecessary details in shared areas.

Part 4 — A Strength-Based Psychosocial Interview

Use a structure such as SSHADESS or HEEADSSS while allowing natural conversation: strengths, school, home, activities, diet and body image, emotions, sleep, substances, sexuality, safety, violence, and online life. Interview in a nonjudgmental manner and normalize questions.

Ask behavior before labels: partners and sexual practices rather than identity alone; frequency, quantity, route, context, and consequences for substances; access to weapons; driving and passenger behavior; bullying; coercion; housing and food security; and trusted adults.

Part 5 — Depression and Suicide Safety

Use a validated adolescent depression tool at recommended preventive intervals and whenever concern exists. A positive screen is not the diagnosis; assess duration, impairment, bipolar symptoms, trauma, substances, medical contributors, psychosis, and supports. Screening is ethical only when the practice has a response pathway.

Ask directly about passive death wish, suicidal thoughts, plan, intent, access to lethal means, past attempts, self-harm, agitation, intoxication, and protective factors. Current intent, inability to maintain safety, severe agitation, psychosis, or medically serious attempt requires emergency intervention and continuous supervision. A “no-suicide contract” does not replace a collaborative safety plan and lethal-means counseling.

Part 6 — Substance Use

Screen with a validated age-appropriate tool. Ask nicotine and vaping, alcohol, cannabis, prescription misuse, opioids, stimulants, inhalants, performance substances, and polysubstance use. Clarify driving, overdose, withdrawal, school, legal, sexual, and mental-health consequences.

Provide brief intervention, motivational interviewing, harm reduction, naloxone when opioid exposure risk exists, and treatment referral. Respiratory depression, severe intoxication, psychosis, chest pain after stimulant use, or dangerous withdrawal requires emergency care. Punitive disclosure can drive avoidance; follow confidentiality law while prioritizing safety.

Part 7 — Sexual and Reproductive Health

Ask whether the adolescent has partners, what body parts are involved, pregnancy potential, contraception, condom use, coercion, pain, bleeding, and STI history. Use inclusive anatomy-based language. Offer vaccines, contraception counseling, condoms, emergency contraception, pregnancy testing, and STI/HIV screening based on current guidance and exposure sites.

CDC recommends routine STI screening for sexually active adolescents according to anatomy, age, behaviors, pregnancy, and risk. Extragenital testing may be needed based on exposure. A negative test does not replace prevention counseling, and a positive test requires treatment, partner strategy, retesting when indicated, and confidentiality-safe contact.

Part 8 — Consent and Coercion

Assess whether sexual activity is wanted, freely chosen, age-concordant under applicable law, and free of pressure, exploitation, trafficking, intoxication, or reproductive control. Ask whether anyone exchanges sex for housing, money, food, substances, or safety. Use a trauma-informed multidisciplinary pathway and mandatory reporting where required.

Acute assault requires time-sensitive options for forensic care, pregnancy prevention, STI prophylaxis, HIV postexposure prophylaxis, injury care, and advocacy. Do not conduct a detailed investigative interview that could retraumatize or compromise forensic assessment.

Part 9 — Eating Disorders and Body Image

Eating disorders occur at every body size, sex, gender, race, and athletic level. Ask restriction, bingeing, vomiting, laxatives, compulsive exercise, fear foods, body dissatisfaction, weight change, dizziness, syncope, menstrual change, constipation, cold intolerance, and family observations. Avoid praising weight loss before understanding how it occurred.

Assess orthostatic vital signs, temperature, heart rate, hydration, growth trajectory, pubertal development, and indicated electrolytes, glucose, phosphorus, magnesium, renal and liver function, blood count, thyroid studies, pregnancy test, and ECG. Bradycardia, hypotension, hypothermia, syncope, significant electrolyte abnormality, prolonged QT, acute food refusal, or suicidality may require hospitalization.

Part 10 — Sleep, School, and Digital Health

Assess sleep duration and schedule, insomnia, snoring, daytime sleepiness, late-night devices, caffeine, school demands, attendance, grades, learning needs, bullying, and work. Sleep loss can mimic or worsen depression, inattention, headaches, and substance use.

Discuss online harassment, sextortion, image sharing, gambling, misinformation, and social comparison without demanding total device removal. Create specific boundaries and identify a trusted adult for unsafe online contact.

Part 11 — Physical Health and Prevention

Use the current Bright Futures periodicity and CDC immunization schedules for blood pressure, growth and BMI trajectory, vision, hearing, oral health, depression and suicide screening, lipid and other risk-based testing, and immunizations including HPV, meningococcal, Tdap, influenza, COVID-19, and catch-up doses.

Sports participation assessment targets exertional chest pain or syncope, unexplained dyspnea, family sudden death, concussion, musculoskeletal injury, asthma control, heat risk, and sickle-cell considerations. Exertional syncope or chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before clearance.

Part 12 — Gender-Affirming and Inclusive Care

Ask name, pronouns, and what language the adolescent uses for their body. Distinguish identity from distress and assess family, school, and community safety. Provide evidence-based, nonstigmatizing care and appropriate specialty support without assuming every health concern is related to gender.

Bullying, family rejection, and discrimination elevate mental-health risk. Screening should be paired with tangible support and crisis planning.

Part 13 — Chronic-Disease Transition

Transition readiness includes knowing diagnoses, medications, allergies, refill process, emergency plan, insurance, pharmacy, appointment scheduling, and how to communicate independently. Begin gradually rather than transferring responsibility abruptly at age 18.

For developmental disability or complex illness, assess decision-making capacity, supported decision-making, guardianship alternatives, and adult-system access while preserving as much autonomy as possible.

Part 14 — Disposition and Follow-Up

Routine outpatient care is appropriate when the adolescent is medically and psychiatrically stable and the follow-up plan protects confidentiality. Same-day evaluation is warranted for escalating depression, suspected eating disorder, STI complication, pregnancy with pain or bleeding, significant intoxication, or unsafe home or relationship conditions.

Emergency care is required for imminent suicide or violence risk, psychosis with danger, overdose, severe withdrawal, sexual assault with acute needs, ectopic-pregnancy concern, hemodynamic instability, eating-disorder instability, or serious injury. Do not send a suicidal adolescent home merely with a referral phone number.

Clinical Case 1 — Confidentiality Creates the Diagnosis

A 16-year-old reports stomachaches only after private time begins, then discloses vaping, missed periods, and coerced sex. The FNP explains limits, assesses immediate safety and pregnancy, offers time-sensitive reproductive and STI care, and activates safeguarding support according to law.

Clinical Case 2 — A Normal BMI Does Not Exclude Instability

A 15-year-old at a midrange BMI has rapid weight loss, compulsive exercise, dizziness, bradycardia, and orthostatic symptoms. The FNP evaluates medical instability and eating disorder urgently rather than reassuring based on BMI alone.

Clinical Case 3 — Positive Depression Screen

A 14-year-old has a positive screen and reports a suicide plan with access to a firearm. The FNP maintains supervision, engages emergency mental-health evaluation, involves caregivers as required for safety, and addresses lethal-means restriction rather than scheduling routine therapy weeks later.

FNP High-Yield Framework: TEENS

  1. T — Tell the privacy rules: private time, legal limits, safe contacts, portal and billing risks.
  2. E — Elicit strengths and exposures: home, school, mood, substances, sexuality, safety, digital life.
  3. E — Evaluate medical and psychiatric stability: suicide, eating disorder, pregnancy, assault, intoxication.
  4. N — Navigate prevention: vaccines, STI/HIV, contraception, sleep, sports, chronic disease.
  5. S — Secure follow-up: confidential results, family support when safe, referral ownership, crisis plan.

Take-Home Summary

Adolescent care depends on trust supported by real privacy systems and clear safety limits. A strength-based interview reveals risks that a routine checklist may miss. Screening must lead to action, and imminent self-harm, exploitation, assault, pregnancy emergency, overdose, or eating-disorder instability requires immediate intervention.

Educational note: Follow current AAP confidentiality and preventive-care policy, CDC immunization and STI guidance, state minor-consent and reporting law, and local psychiatric and emergency protocols. Imminent self-harm or violence, assault, trafficking, overdose, psychosis, unstable eating disorder, or pregnancy emergency requires urgent care.
